system.name: LS S6 Y11/Y12 Features of ancient societies

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students participate in a historical investigation to further develop their skills and make real-world and personal connections to history. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest and be developed to meet students’ learning needs.

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated as appropriate.

The Historical investigation focus area is designed to provide students with opportunities to engage in historical inquiry and develop research and communication skills.

Possible historical investigations could include:

  • local or national Aboriginal sites of significance and/or interest
  • the ways sources reveal information about a society, movement, people, groups or events
  • the cause and/or impact of a historical event
  • the significance of a historical development
  • using sources to explain how historical opinions have changed over time for significant people, places or events
  • comparing and contrasting sources with different perspectives
  • the contribution of a historical site or artefact in helping to explain the past
  • perspectives on an individual, group or event over time
  • the accuracy of modern representations of specific historical events
  • an exploration of personal connections such as the contrast between a specific ancient society and modern life
  • contemporary issues around preserving/conserving the past, world heritage, tourism, museums, archaeology, site studies or virtual tours.

web_content_rtb__content.value:
The Ancient History 11–12 Syllabus aligns with the Ancient History Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus to provide opportunities for integrated delivery.

Organisation of Ancient History 11–12

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Ancient History 11–12.

Image long description: A list of historical concepts and historical skills sit in the middle of the diagram, each surrounded by a box. Historical concepts are: Causation; Continuity and change; Perspectives; Significance; and Contestability. Historical skills are: Analysis and use of sources; Historical interpretation; Historical investigation and research; and Explanation and communication. The syllabus is separated into 3 focus areas for Year 11, and 4 focus areas for Year 12. The focus areas for Year 11 are: Investigating ancient history; Features of ancient societies; and Historical investigation. The focus areas for Year 12 are: Cities of Vesuvius: Pompeii and Herculaneum; Ancient societies; Historical personalities; and Historical periods.

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement Ancient History learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Ancient History 11–12 focuses on developing student understanding of the ancient past and how it was shaped by people and events. The course offers students opportunities to engage with written and physical sources from the past, developing students' analysis and reasoning skills.

What students learn

Through the study of Ancient History 11–12, students learn to:

  • develop an understanding of historical causation and the ways in which human societies have changed over time
  • develop an understanding of the variety of perspectives that have been and are held about the past
  • develop skills in analysis and reasoning to make judgements about the significance of various people and events in the past and form their own conclusions about the nature of historical development
  • construct logical and cogent historical arguments about the past, supported by evidence.

Course structure and requirements

Year 11 course structure and requirements

The Year 11 Ancient History course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 3 focus areas.
Year 11 focus areasIndicative hours

Investigating ancient history

  • The nature of ancient history
  • Case studies

Each case study should be a minimum of 10 indicative hours.

60
Features of ancient societies40 (minimum)
Historical investigation20 (maximum)

Studies undertaken in the Year 11 course should be selected from a range of societies.

Content may be integrated across the 3 focus areas of the course in the development of a teaching and learning program.

Investigating ancient history

  • The nature of ancient history
  • Case studies

Students undertake:

  • at least ONE option from The nature of ancient history, AND
  • at least TWO case studies
  • ONE case study must be from Egypt, Greece, Rome or Celtic Europe
  • ONE case study must be from Australia, Asia, the Near East or the Americas.

The list in the Investigating ancient history – Case studies focus area of this syllabus provides case study options teachers may use.

Case studies are investigations into historical features, people, places, events and developments of the ancient world. They are oriented towards the problems and issues of investigating the past.

Case studies in the Year 11 course are intended to provide students with opportunities to:

  • study the various ways in which historians and archaeologists investigate and construct the past, the types of questions they ask, the explanations they give and the issues they raise
  • analyse and interpret archaeological and written sources
  • generate hypotheses and weigh up contemporary theories and explanations on the basis of the available evidence.

Case studies can provide a historical context in which students learn about relevant methods and issues.

Case studies must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Ancient History or History Extension courses.

Features of ancient societies

Students study at least TWO ancient societies through an investigation of:

  • a different key feature for each society, OR
  • one key feature across the societies selected.

A range of possible options is provided in the Features of ancient societies focus area of this syllabus.

Learning in the focus area of Features of ancient societies is concerned with seeking explanations of the ‘how’ and ‘why’ questions of history. This includes an interpretation of the evidence for how people lived in the past and why they may have lived that way. This focus area provides students with opportunities to develop an understanding of:

  • the nature, range and limitations of the available sources
  • the social history of a people through an investigation of the remains of their material culture
  • significant developments, forces or individuals that may have shaped the selected feature(s).

Options selected must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Ancient History or History Extension courses.

Historical investigation

The Historical investigation is designed to further develop relevant investigative, research and communication skills. The investigation may be undertaken as a standalone study or integrated into any other focus area in the Year 11 course. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest. It may be conducted individually or collaboratively.

The investigation must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Ancient History or History Extension courses.

Historical concepts and skills

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated throughout the course. The various studies and options provide the contexts through which concepts and skills are to be developed. These help guide students when engaging in historical analysis and argument.

Year 12 course structure and requirements

The Year 12 Ancient History course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 4 focus areas
  • Core study: Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum
  • ONE Ancient societies option
  • ONE Historical personalities option
  • ONE Historical periods option.
Year 12 focus areasIndicative hours
Core study: Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum30
Ancient societies30
Historical personalities30
Historical periods30

The Year 12 course requires study from at least TWO of the following areas:

  • Egypt
  • Near East
  • China
  • Greece
  • Rome.

The Core study: Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum is a Roman study.

Options in the Year 12 course contain a Context content group. This content group should be taught in a maximum of 3 hours.

Historical concepts and skills

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated throughout the course. The options provide the contexts through which concepts and skills are to be developed. These help guide students when engaging in historical analysis and argument.

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Ancient History 11–12 Syllabus.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Ancient History Life Skills 11–12 provides opportunities for students to explore the people, groups and events of the ancient past and how they have influenced past societies and the world today. Students develop skills in locating, selecting, organising, planning and presenting information within a historical context. Students develop knowledge and understanding to contribute as active and informed citizens.

What students learn

Through the study of Ancient History Life Skills 11–12, students:

  • explore key events, developments, movements, individuals and groups of the ancient past to develop an understanding of how these have impacted our world
  • examine features of the ancient past, such as beliefs and practices, social and political organisation, art and architecture, culture and trade, and power and warfare, and consider how these have contributed to our world
  • develop knowledge and skills in historical inquiry by participating in historical investigations
  • pose questions, gather evidence, process information, draw conclusions and communicate their understanding about the past
  • develop an appreciation of diverse perspectives and ideas.

Course structure

Ancient History Life Skills Year 11 and Year 12

The following focus areas can be studied throughout Year 11 (120 hours) and Year 12 (120 hours).

  • Investigating ancient history – The nature of ancient history; Case studies
  • Features of ancient societies
  • Historical investigation
  • Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum
  • Ancient societies
  • Historical personalities
  • Historical periods

For Ancient History Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Ancient History Life Skills
    11–12 outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The outcomes describe the knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of teaching and learning. Teachers should use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content included in each focus area.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Ancient History Life Skills 11–12 outcomes and content, and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • The content for historical concepts and skills should be integrated throughout the course.
  • The Historical investigation can be integrated into any aspect of the course or undertaken as a discrete focus area for students with specific areas of historical interest. The investigation can be undertaken collaboratively or independently. Students can do parts of an investigation or a complete investigation.
  • Examples provided in the content are suggestions only. Teachers may use the examples provided or other examples to meet the particular needs of individual students.
Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Ancient History Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus.

content.value:
Students study at least TWO case studies, choosing ONE from List A and ONE from List B. The studies may incorporate methods and issues involved in investigating the ancient past, as relevant.

Teachers may develop their own case studies. These may be designed to provide a context for options selected in the Year 12 course. However, case studies must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Ancient History or History Extension courses. Teacher-developed case studies must follow the geographical division indicated in Lists A and B.

  • List B: The Shang dynasty

Students discuss contemporary methods and issues involved in the investigation of ancient history through a study of at least ONE of the following focus area options:

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
The following case studies are suggestions only. Teachers may develop ideas and concepts from these case studies to support student interests and abilities. Students may participate in a single case study, part of a case study, or elements of content as appropriate.

Case studies from Egypt, Greece, Rome and Celtic Europe

  • Old Kingdom Egypt
  • Tutankhamun’s tomb
  • Deir el-Medina
  • Alexandria
  • Thera
  • Troy
  • The Roman games
  • The Celts
  • Boudicca
  • The Valley of the Queens
  • Mycenae
  • Greek drama
  • The Etruscans
  • The impact of expansion on Rome
  • Tiberius Gracchus
  • The city of Rome
  • Roman Britain

Case studies from Australia, Asia, the Near East and the Americas

  • Ancient Australia
  • The Shang dynasty
  • Ashoka
  • Nineveh
  • Persepolis
  • Civilisations of the river – Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley
  • Masada
  • Palmyra and the Silk Road
  • Teotihuacan
  • Jericho
  • Lachish
  • The Akkadian Empire
  • Carthage
  • Hannibal and the Punic Wars
  • The Battle of Red Cliffs
  • The Moche
  • The early Maya

Teachers may develop their own case studies, where appropriate, to meet student interests and abilities. If they do so, they should consider the following aspects in their case study:

  • relevance to the present
  • key historical features and issues
  • the roles of individuals and groups within their chosen context
  • key events and/or developments, and how they shape the past
  • the significance of the site, individual or society
  • impact and legacy

content.value:
Purpose

Exploring archaeological sites and historical sources enables students to develop the skills needed to learn about the past. When engaging with artefacts, images and stories, students develop an understanding that people, places and events can be interpreted and represented in different ways. Students develop interpersonal skills such as empathy and appreciation for diverse perspectives, including ethical perspectives relating to the ownership of sites, artefacts and sources.

Designing teaching and learning

The Investigating ancient history focus area consists of 2 parts – The nature of ancient history and Case studies. The nature of ancient history introduces students to the nature and use of ancient sites, artefacts and sources. Students can then apply their learning to Case studies.

Focus of study

Content for study can be selected in the following ways.

Selecting a single option for study from The nature of ancient history. For example:

  • The investigation of sites and sources, e.g. Piltdown man, The Dead Sea Scrolls or Petra
  • The representation of the ancient past, e.g. Ramesses II, Babylon, The Amazons
  • Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites, e.g. Giza, the site of the Terracotta Warriors in Xian, a recent example of a site at risk
  • Cultural heritage and the role of museums, e.g. Bust of Nefertiti, Priam’s treasure, Indigenous collections
  • The treatment and display of human remains, e.g. Ötzi ‘the Iceman’, Mummified remains of ancient Egypt, Mungo Man and/or Mungo Woman.

Selecting 2 or more options for study from The nature of ancient history. For example:

  • The investigation of ancient sites and sources: archaeology and The representation of the ancient past: real sources, fakes and forgeries
  • The investigation of ancient sites and sources: limitations and reliability of sources and Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites: conservation and reconstruction.

Selecting one or more option from The nature of ancient history AND one option from Case studies. For example:

  • The representation of the ancient past – Troy
  • Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites – Persepolis
  • Cultural heritage and the role of museums – Ancient Australia
  • The treatment and display of human remains – Tutankhamun’s tomb

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about how sources can be used to ask and answer questions about the past, the outcome requires students to use sources to form conclusions. Students use images of the ancient footprints discovered at Lake Mungo to draw conclusions, such as: ‘Who made the footprints?’, ‘What were the people doing at the time the footprints were made?’, ‘How old are the footprints?’

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Perspective, significance and contestability – whose perspectives are represented in sources, how reliable are sites and sources in giving us information about the past.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • The representation of the ancient past: Representation
    • Sources that demonstrate how a person, site, society or event has been represented over time
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Access historical ideas and representations
    • Compare different historical ideas and representations
Teachers engage students with an image, a film clip and a website about the gladiator games in ancient Rome and guide discussion about what information can be gained. Students use a word bank to select a word that best describes the representation of the gladiators in each of the sources, e.g. hero, victim, warrior, slave, killer.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same option within Investigating ancient history, but the depth and scope of content will differ. For example, when studying the Cultural heritage and the role of museums option, students studying Ancient History may look at an entire collection to understand the role of museums in acquiring, storing and exhibiting artefacts and cultural materials, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might focus on one artefact and how it was collected and displayed.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This teaching advice applies to the 2 Investigating ancient history focus areas and is applicable for all options.

The Investigating ancient history focus area consists of 2 parts. The nature of ancient history introduces students to the methods and issues of constructing history. Students then apply this understanding in the Case studies.

Students develop targeted historical skills including the analysis and use of sources, historical interpretation, explanation and communication. Using the discipline-based process of historical inquiry, students analyse sources for evidence, which they then use to develop claims about the past, considering key concepts such as perspectives and contestability. Using these reasoned claims, students explain and communicate their understanding through historical accounts and arguments.

Selecting one case study from each of List A and List B allows students to develop and apply historical skills to a diverse range of ancient societies, historical events and personalities. Consider students’ backgrounds, interests and access to source material when selecting case study options.

Designing teaching and learning

Integrating historical concepts and skills

Historical concepts provide the framework through which students develop their understanding of the complexities of the past and the way it has been interpreted through time. They allow students to engage with historical thinking and form their own increasingly perceptive interpretations of historical events, ideas and forces. Teachers select the appropriate concepts on which to focus that align closely with their chosen content options. Some concepts will lend themselves more readily to specific options than others.

Use of sources

Sources are the key to any inquiry into the past and form the basis for historical analysis and interpretation. Using sources, students engage with a variety of perspectives as evidence to inform their understanding of the past. When selecting sources for teaching and learning activities, teachers should use and model ethical practices, such as the consideration of copyright and intellectual property acknowledgement, heritage issues, and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) concerns, to ensure students understand the importance of engaging appropriately when using historical source material. Select source material carefully to cater for the needs of the students in the class, considering accessibility needs and issues such as the availability of audio and/or closed captions with videos, and of other materials such as tactile objects and replicas of maps and artefacts.

Historical inquiry

Historical inquiry is an active process that allows students to develop and enact the historical skills required to engage with history as a discipline. Through the historical inquiry process, students question, analyse, interpret, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. The historical inquiry process involves students going through the steps of acquiring, processing and communicating in order to demonstrate their application of substantive and conceptual historical understanding.

Teaching and learning activities in Investigating ancient history should be designed to support students to make evidence-based arguments exploring historical concepts such as causation, significance, and continuity and change. For example, activities which compare and contrast a range of historical sources about an event will support students to engage with these concepts and to develop source-analysis skills. This in turn will encourage more rigorous interpretations. Selecting sources from a wide range of perspectives will develop students’ knowledge base, which will ensure a stronger foundation for analysis and interpretation throughout the focus area.

To illustrate the content of the selected option(s) teachers may choose to use examples from the list below, develop their own investigations, or integrate their study with content from Case studies or an option from the focus area of Features of ancient societies. The following examples are suggestions only.

The investigation of ancient sites and sources

  • The Theban Mapping Project
  • Marine archaeology
  • The Piltdown man
  • Priam’s treasure
  • The Dead Sea Scrolls
  • Homer’s Iliad
  • Selected excerpts from Herodotus or Thucydides
  • Petra
  • The Nazca Lines
  • Lord of Sipán
  • Plain of Jars

The representation of the ancient past

  • Ramesses II
  • Leonidas I
  • Hannibal
  • Zenobia
  • The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
  • Babylon
  • The Persians
  • The Celts
  • The Amazons

Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites

  • Giza
  • Knossos
  • The Athenian Agora
  • Persepolis
  • Palmyra
  • Teotihuacan
  • The site of the Terracotta Warriors in Xi’an
  • A recent example of a site at risk

Cultural heritage and the role of museums

  • The bust of Nefertiti
  • Parthenon sculptures
  • Crowther’s collection
  • Priam’s treasure
  • The Benin Bronzes
  • Indigenous collections

The treatment and display of human remains

  • Ötzi (the Iceman)
  • Bog bodies
  • The Tarim mummies
  • Mummified remains of ancient Egypt
  • Mungo Man and/or Mungo Woman

The focus areas in Year 11 may be integrated to suit the needs of students. For example:

  • An option from the focus area The nature of ancient history can be integrated into Case studies or into the focus area Features of ancient societies. For example, content from The investigation of ancient sites and sources might be integrated with content from the case study on Troy. Alternatively, content from The representation of the ancient past might be integrated with content from Features of ancient societies – for instance, examining representations of ancient Greek women in modern media.
  • Teachers may also select individual content points from several options in The nature of ancient history and teach these as a standalone option or integrate with Case studies or Features of ancient societies.

Purpose

Learning about an ancient society helps students to develop an appreciation for different ways of life, including religious beliefs, leadership and culture. Students learn to be open to new ideas and develop appreciation for how an ancient society has influenced aspects of the way we live today.

Students have opportunities to develop skills in chronology, the use of maps, reading and interpreting sources, and communicating and sharing ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One ancient society is selected for study. Consider elements of the content appropriate for the society selected.

For example:

  • New Kingdom Egypt to the death of Amenhotep III – arts and culture and the legacy of Amenhotep III
  • New Kingdom Egypt during the Ramesside period – trade and the expansion of wealth
  • Israel from Solomon to the fall of Samaria – the siege on Samaria
  • Persia in the time of Darius and Xerxes – the Persian Wars
  • China during the Han dynasty – scientific and technological advancements
  • Minoan Crete in the Bronze Age – palaces and art
  • Sparta to the Battle of Leuctra 371 BCE – life in Sparta and the nature and role of the military
  • Athens in the time of Pericles – democracy and citizenship

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the structure of government in Athens in the time of Pericles, the outcome requires students to investigate people, events or developments. Students can investigate the event of Pericles’ fight against the council of leaders, the Areopagus, and how this contributed to a more democratic society.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about features of ancient societies. For example, when studying trade and the expansion of wealth in New Kingdom Egypt, begin with students recognising food, clothing and other goods that are regularly purchased.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • continuity and change – role of men and women in the ancient society and today
  • significance – legacies from the ancient society, such as democracy, warfare, architecture.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Ancient societies: Cultural life
    • Examples of art and architecture
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical investigation and research
    • Make personal connections to people, places, artefacts and events of interest
Teachers show students examples of Minoan art, including paintings, frescoes and pottery. Students are guided to identify familiar animals represented. Students find other examples of art that they like, featuring the same or similar animals and communicate why they think animals are often featured in artworks throughout history.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same society, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying Athens in the time of Pericles, students studying Ancient History may analyse continuity and change in the structure and features of government, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might identify key events in Pericles’ political life.

Purpose

Exploring the archaeological sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum enables students to further develop their understanding of what sites and sources can tell us about the past. When exploring artefacts, images and accounts, students can develop an appreciation for life in the ancient past.

Students have opportunities to develop skills in using maps, reading and interpreting sources as well as an empathy for different perspectives and ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about life in Pompeii and Herculaneum compared with life today, the outcome requires students to identify connections between the past and the present. Students can create a Venn diagram to identify differences in one aspect of life, such as the everyday life of a citizen.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about Pompeii and Herculaneum. For example, students identify objects they use in daily life and identify what this would tell someone in the future about present society. This will help them make connections with artefacts explored from Pompeii or Herculaneum.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • causation – effects of the volcanic eruption
  • continuity and change – how daily life today is similar and different to daily life in Pompeii or Herculaneum
  • contestability – what we don’t know about Pompeii or Herculaneum because of a lack of evidence.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Cites of Vesuvius: Archaeology at Pompeii and Herculaneum
    • The importance of reconstruction of these sites
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Communicate about the significance of historical people, places or event(s)

Teachers use reconstructions of Pompeii to identify important features of the city.

Students create a visual image, multimodal presentation or speech to communicate why reconstructions of this site are important for people today.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students can study the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when exploring archaeological practices students studying Ancient History may assess the practices and challenges of excavation and conservation, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might identify how one or more specific artefacts were discovered and excavated.

Purpose

Learning about ancient societies supports students to develop an understanding of and appreciation for aspects of our current society, such as roles of men and women, leadership, and religious beliefs and practices. When students explore societies that are different from today, it can help them to be open to different perspectives and ideas.

Students have opportunities to develop skills in numeracy (time, sequencing, location and navigation) and literacy (reading and interpreting sources, creating texts) when exploring various features of ancient societies.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

The focus of study may be:

  • an ancient society and one or more key features
  • a key feature across one or more ancient societies
  • comparison of the key features of an ancient society with the key features of modern society.

For example:

Ancient societyKey featureComparative study
  • Egypt – Slavery; Power and image
  • Israel – Art and architecture
  • Greece – Art and architecture
  • Rome – Power and image
  • India – Death and funerary customs
  • China – Trade and cultural contact
  • Women (roles and status)
  • Slavery (treatment, roles, duties and freedom)
  • Art and architecture
  • Weapons and warfare
  • Death and funerary customs
  • Power and image (ruling hierarchy)
  • Trade and cultural contact (main items of trade and trading partners)
  • Duties of men and women
  • Governance and power
  • Leisure and entertainment
  • Rights and freedoms
  • Military, weapons and warfare
  • Types of houses or dwellings
  • Daily life
  • Traditions, customs and beliefs

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the everyday life of women in the society, the outcome requires students to describe features of places or societies in the ancient world. Students can engage with images or stories about the roles of women in ancient Egypt, identify some common tasks performed, then choose one of the tasks and select adjectives to complete a sentence cloze to describe the task.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about features of ancient societies. For example, when studying power and image in an ancient society, begin with students identifying familiar leaders in their own lives, such as parents, teachers, police and the roles these leaders have.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • causation – effects of trade on ancient societies
  • continuity and change – role of women in the ancient past and today
  • significance – legacies from ancient societies that still exist today, such as architecture, weapons and warfare.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Features of ancient societies: Trade and cultural contact
    • The types of art and architecture that characterised the ancient society
    • Different styles of art and materials used
  • Historical concepts and skills: Analysis and use of sources
    • Access a variety of sources
    • Identify relevant information from a range of sources

Teachers provide images of artworks from ancient Greece and guide students to identify common materials, symbols, patterns or styles used.

Students create or curate a collection of artefacts that represent ancient Greece, incorporating the materials, symbols, patterns or styles identified from sources.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same society or features of societies, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the role of women, students studying Ancient History may explain the significance of particular roles and analyse different perspectives, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might identify and describe roles.

Purpose

Engaging in a historical investigation enables students to develop critical thinking skills as they determine what information is useful and reliable, and use that information to support an opinion or argument. When working collaboratively with others, students can build interpersonal skills such as empathy, appreciation of diverse perspectives and the ability to share opinions and ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

This focus area can be integrated into any aspect of the Ancient History Life Skills course to further explore an area of interest. A student may complete all, part or selected aspects of an investigation. The investigation can be done as a class, in small groups or independently.

The historical inquiry process is central to the Historical investigation and is articulated in the content groups. The steps include:

  • posing and responding to a question about the past
  • gathering primary and secondary sources of evidence
  • processing and analysing information
  • drawing conclusions
  • communicating understanding.

In addition to this, students may need to consolidate their understanding of history through personal connections before beginning the historical inquiry process.

Historical concepts and skills

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. Understanding the concept of perspective, for example, is critical to determining which source material is useful and reliable.

Historical skills should be integrated and may be selected to meet the individual needs of students. For example, one student might focus on placing events related to the investigation in chronological order while another student finds important information about an event.

Selecting a historical investigation

The scope and nature of the investigation can be adjusted to align with students’ strengths, interests, needs and goals, or to overlap with another focus area.

Teaching and learning strategies

Explicit teaching

  • Teach students to first order events according to the year. Next, order events within the same year by month, and then date.
  • Provide modelled, guided and independent practice in locating historical sources online by determining key words for a search and selecting a reliable website from the search results.

Scaffolds

  • Provide a template for students to use to organise information from sources, including where it is from, when it originated, who the author or creator is, why it was written or made, and what information it conveys.
  • Provide students with a graphic organiser to support their communication of continuity and change within the investigation, such as a Venn diagram or T-chart.

Feedback

  • Provide students with explicit feedback to direct and redirect the inquiry. For example, provide feedback to help students formulate inquiry questions that will provide enough scope for an investigation without being too broad.
  • Provide explicit feedback on when and how to use historical terms and concepts.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students can participate in an historical investigation, but the scope of the investigation and the amount of scaffolding and support provided will differ. For example, students studying Ancient History locate sources independently, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills may select from a curated set of sources targeted to their level of understanding.

Purpose

The period of time in history, the key personalities of historical significance and the society in which they lived, exerted their influence and left a legacy to today is a path to pursue an interest in history. The examination of a personality, a society or a period of time in history does not happen in isolation, but in an integrated way. This study can therefore emphasis the aspects that are of most relevance and interest.

Teachers may decide to study the 3 focus areas separately, studying selected ancient societies, selected historical personalities and selected historical periods based on student interests and contextual considerations. Teachers also may consider an integrated approach to the study of ancient societies and/or historical personalities and/or historical periods.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One historical period is selected for study, with a focus on the nature of power and authority and significant developments of the period. Consider elements of the content appropriate for the society selected.

For example:

  • New Kingdom Egypt to the death of Thutmose IV – the rule of the pharaohs in New Kingdom Egypt and how they used power
  • New Kingdom Egypt – Amenhotep III to the death of Ramesses II – women’s roles of power, including wives, queens, deities
  • The Levant in the period c. 869–586 BCE – the reign of Hezekiah and his influence on religion
  • Persia – Cyrus II to the death of Darius III – the strengthening and expansion of the Persian empire under Darius I
  • Imperial China – the Qin and Han 247–87 BCE – comparison of the power and authority of the Qin and Han dynasties
  • The Greek world 500–440 BCE – the Persian Wars and Greek victory
  • Greece from 404 BCE to the death of Philip II – Philip II and the Macedonian expansion into Greece
  • The fall of the Roman Republic 78–42 BCE – Caesar’s dictatorship and assassination
  • The Augustan Age 44 BCE–14 CE – the political power of Augustus Caesar
  • The Julio-Claudians 14–68 CE – Roman emperors of the Julio-Claudian dynasty

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the role and status of women in New Kingdom Egypt, the outcome requires students to describe features of places or societies in the ancient world. Students can engage with sources to explore the status women held in society through their roles. Students use a word bank to create a written or multimodal text that describes two influential roles for women.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about features of ancient societies. For example, when studying the Persian Wars and Greece, students identify on a map the geographical region and identify any connections they have with those regions today.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • causation – reasons for individual people’s rise to power, or shifts in power
  • continuity and change – changes in power and authority during the historical period; structures of government that have continued into the modern world.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Historical periods: Social, political and economic events and developments
    • Role of the military and key conflicts
  • Historical concepts and skills: Analysis and use of sources
    • Identify relevant information from a range of sources
    • Organise information from sources
Teachers provide sources to guide students to identify key events in the military career of Philip II. Using extracts from the sources, students locate information to answer the question: ‘what made Philip II’s military actions successful?’ Students organise information in a mind map, categorising key facts under ‘weapons’, ‘tactics’, ‘army’.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same historical period, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the period of the Julio-Claudians 14–68 CE, students studying Ancient History may assess the role and significance of the Julio-Claudian dynasty in the development of the principate, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might identify the chronology of rulers of the Julio-Claudian dynasty and investigate key events in the leadership of selected rulers.

Purpose

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One historical personality is selected for study. Students can engage with the life of the personality from birth to death, or specific aspects of the personality’s life.

For example:

  • Egypt – Hatshepsut
  • Egypt – Akhenaten
  • The Near East – Xerxes
  • China – Qin Shi Huangdi
  • Greece – Pericles
  • Greece – Alexander the Great
  • Rome – Julius Caesar
  • Rome – Agrippina the Younger

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about Akhenaten’s rise to power, the outcome requires students to recognise causes and effects of events or developments. Students engage with the story of Akhenaten’s early life, then select from a series of captioned images (e.g. ‘chosen by the Egyptians’, ‘born a pharaoh’, ‘death of his father’) when asked how he became pharaoh.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about features of ancient societies. For example, before engaging with the biography of the selected personality, students create a timeline of significant events in their own lives. Students can also be encouraged to make connections with events in the lives of the historical personality and their own life. For example, being the only daughter or son in a family, caring for younger siblings, receiving an award for an achievement, negotiating a disagreement with a friend or family member.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • causation – the influence of the Persian wars on Pericles
  • continuity and change – the continuation of the Chinese dynasties after the rule of Qin Shihuangdi
  • significance – the yearly calendar was started by Julius Caesar.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Historical personalities: Background
    • Biographical details of the selected personality
  • Historical concepts and skills: Time and chronology
    • Use chronology to order people, places, changes and events from the past
    • Use the language of time
Teachers guide students to identify key events in the life of a historical personality. Students place the key events in chronological order, with or without a timeline. They use the language of time to recount biographical details, for example ‘first Alexander the Great freed the Greeks from Persian rule’, ‘he took Egypt from the Persians before he captured Babylon’.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same historical personality, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the differing interpretations and representations of Xerxes, students studying Ancient History may evaluate the accuracy and reliability of representations of him as a military leader, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might identify perspectives of Xerxes in popular culture, such as the graphic novel 300 and the video games Assassin’s creed odyssey and Civilization II and III.

Purpose

Exploring archaeological sites and historical sources enables students to develop the skills needed to learn about the past. When engaging with artefacts, images and stories, students develop an understanding that people, places and events can be interpreted and represented in different ways. Students develop interpersonal skills such as empathy and appreciation for diverse perspectives, including ethical perspectives relating to the ownership of sites, artefacts and sources.

Designing teaching and learning

The Investigating ancient history focus area consists of 2 parts – The nature of ancient history and Case studies. The nature of ancient history introduces students to the nature and use of ancient sites, artefacts and sources. Students can then apply their learning to Case studies.

Focus of study

Content for study can be selected in the following ways.

Selecting a single option for study from The nature of ancient history. For example:

  • The investigation of sites and sources, e.g. Piltdown man, The Dead Sea Scrolls or Petra
  • The representation of the ancient past, e.g. Ramesses II, Babylon, The Amazons
  • Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites, e.g. Giza, the site of the Terracotta Warriors in Xian, a recent example of a site at risk
  • Cultural heritage and the role of museums, e.g. Bust of Nefertiti, Priam’s treasure, Indigenous collections
  • The treatment and display of human remains, e.g. Ötzi ‘the Iceman’, Mummified remains of ancient Egypt, Mungo Man and/or Mungo Woman.

Selecting 2 or more options for study from The nature of ancient history. For example:

  • The investigation of ancient sites and sources: archaeology and The representation of the ancient past: real sources, fakes and forgeries
  • The investigation of ancient sites and sources: limitations and reliability of sources and Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites: conservation and reconstruction.

Selecting one or more option from The nature of ancient history AND one option from Case studies. For example:

  • The representation of the ancient past – Troy
  • Conservation and reconstruction of ancient sites – Persepolis
  • Cultural heritage and the role of museums – Ancient Australia
  • The treatment and display of human remains – Tutankhamun’s tomb

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about how sources can be used to ask and answer questions about the past, the outcome requires students to use sources to form conclusions. Students use images of the ancient footprints discovered at Lake Mungo to draw conclusions, such as: ‘Who made the footprints?’, ‘What were the people doing at the time the footprints were made?’, ‘How old are the footprints?’

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Perspective, significance and contestability – whose perspectives are represented in sources, how reliable are sites and sources in giving us information about the past.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • The representation of the ancient past: Representation
    • Sources that demonstrate how a person, site, society or event has been represented over time
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Access historical ideas and representations
    • Compare different historical ideas and representations
Teachers engage students with an image, a film clip and a website about the gladiator games in ancient Rome and guide discussion about what information can be gained. Students use a word bank to select a word that best describes the representation of the gladiators in each of the sources, e.g. hero, victim, warrior, slave, killer.

Connecting with Ancient History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Ancient History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Ancient History Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same option within Investigating ancient history, but the depth and scope of content will differ. For example, when studying the Cultural heritage and the role of museums option, students studying Ancient History may look at an entire collection to understand the role of museums in acquiring, storing and exhibiting artefacts and cultural materials, while students studying Ancient History Life Skills might focus on one artefact and how it was collected and displayed.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to consider the causes and effects of developments, the role and significance of events, individuals and groups, continuity and change, and different perspectives of individuals and groups in their historical context.

The thematic approach allows for the application of historical understanding and skills to key feature(s) across 2 ancient societies. Students develop targeted historical skills including the analysis and use of sources, historical interpretation, explanation and communication. Using the discipline-based process of historical inquiry, students analyse sources for evidence, which they then use to develop claims about the past, considering key concepts such as continuity and change, and significance. Using these reasoned claims, students explain and communicate their understanding through historical accounts and arguments.

Designing teaching and learning

Integrating historical concepts and skills

Historical concepts provide the framework through which students develop their understanding of the complexities of the past and the way it has been interpreted through time. They allow students to engage with historical thinking and form their own increasingly perceptive interpretations of historical events, ideas and forces. Teachers select the appropriate concepts on which to focus that align closely with their chosen content options. Some concepts will lend themselves more readily to specific options than others.

Use of sources

Sources are the key to any inquiry into the past and form the basis for historical analysis and interpretation. Using sources, students engage with a variety of perspectives as evidence to inform their understanding of the past. When selecting sources for teaching and learning activities, teachers should use and model ethical practices, such as the consideration of copyright and intellectual property acknowledgement, heritage issues, and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) concerns, to ensure students understand the importance of engaging appropriately when using historical source material. Select source material carefully to cater for the needs of the students in the class, considering accessibility needs and issues such as the availability of audio and/or closed captions with videos, and of other materials such as tactile objects and replicas of maps and artefacts.

Historical inquiry

Historical inquiry is an active process that allows students to develop and enact the historical skills required to engage with history as a discipline. Through the historical inquiry process, students question, analyse, interpret, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. The historical inquiry process involves students going through the steps of acquiring, processing and communicating in order to demonstrate their application of substantive and conceptual historical understanding.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students develop targeted historical skills including the analysis and use of sources, historical interpretation, explanation and communication. Using the discipline-based process of historical inquiry, students analyse sources for evidence, which they then use to develop claims about the past, considering key concepts such as perspectives and contestability. Using these reasoned claims, students explain and communicate their understanding through historical accounts and arguments.

Teachers should provide a range of different types of both primary and secondary sources, so that students can apply and further develop the source-analysis skills learnt in Year 11. Providing a range of sources of varied complexity allows all students, including those with diverse learning needs, to engage in the process of analysis and historical inquiry.

Designing teaching and learning

Integrating historical concepts and skills

Historical concepts provide the framework through which students develop their understanding of the complexities of the past and the way it has been interpreted through time. They allow students to engage with historical thinking and form their own increasingly perceptive interpretations of historical events and forces. Teachers select the appropriate concepts on which to focus that align closely with their chosen content options. Some concepts will lend themselves more readily to specific options than others.

Use of sources

Sources are the key to any inquiry into the past and form the basis for historical analysis and interpretation. Using sources, students engage with a variety of perspectives as evidence to inform their understanding of the past. When selecting sources for teaching and learning activities, teachers should use and model ethical practices, such as the consideration of copyright and intellectual property acknowledgement, heritage issues, and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) concerns, to ensure students understand the importance of engaging appropriately when using historical source material. Select source material carefully to cater for the needs of the students in the class, considering accessibility needs and issues such as the availability of audio and/or closed captions with videos, and of other materials such as tactile objects and replicas of maps and artefacts.

Historical inquiry

Historical inquiry is an active process that allows students to develop and enact the historical skills required to engage with history as a discipline. Through the historical inquiry process, students question, analyse, interpret, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. The historical inquiry process involves students going through the steps of acquiring, processing and communicating in order to demonstrate their application of substantive and conceptual historical understanding.

Teaching and learning activities in Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum should be designed to support students to make evidence-based arguments exploring historical concepts such as causation, significance, and continuity and change. For example, activities which compare and contrast a range of historical sources about an event will support students to engage with these concepts and to develop source-analysis skills. This in turn will encourage more rigorous interpretations. Selecting sources from a wide range of perspectives will develop students’ knowledge base, which will ensure a stronger foundation for analysis and interpretation throughout the focus area.

The Context content group provides information needed for students to understand the Core study and can be taught as a standalone point or integrated with relevant content. For example, the content point ‘The geographical setting and natural features of Campania’ supports student understanding of content points relating to economic activities and health. The ‘Impact of the eruption of 79 CE on Pompeii and Herculaneum’ content point can be related to ‘The nature, range, value and limitations of sources about Pompeii and Herculaneum, including art, buildings, organic remains and writing’, as well as content points in the Archaeology at Pompeii and Herculaneum content group.

Content in the Core study can be integrated. For example, ‘The practices and challenges of excavation and conservation at the sites in the 20th and 21st centuries’ may be taught concurrently with some content in ‘21st-century archaeological issues’, where the selected practices overlap with contemporary issues, such as the destructive nature of excavation or the historical accuracy of reconstructions.

Teachers should identify a range of types of sources, as well as specific sources, from which students can draw evidence to support their explanations or arguments. Some sources will provide evidence which is relevant to more than one content point. For example, teachers may choose to explore the Villa of the Mysteries, which provides evidence related to women, industries, the features and functions of houses and the role of religion.

The content point ‘The nature, range, value and limitations of sources about life in Pompeii and Herculaneum, including art, buildings, organic remains and writing’ can be taught as a standalone point, or integrated with other content points in the Source analysis content group. Limitations of sources could include the number of sources, loss of provenance, the purpose of the source (such as graffiti or inscriptions) or the broader challenge of using archaeological sources to reconstruct life in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Historiographical issues may also be relevant in the analysis of sources.

web_content_rtb__content.value:
Assessment is used to analyse and interpret the knowledge, understanding and skills that students demonstrate throughout the learning process. Assessment provides information about student learning and achievement at a point in time and the progress students have made.

Assessment is most effective when it is an integral part of teaching and learning. The primary role of assessment is to identify where students are in their learning so that teaching can be adapted to target student needs, and progress can be monitored over time.

Schools use syllabuses, assessment and reporting materials and Assessment Certification and Examination (ACE) requirements to develop school-based assessment programs.

Assessment involves:

  •  identifying where students are in their learning
  •  ongoing monitoring of student progress in relation to the syllabus
  •  providing feedback about student progress to determine the next steps in learning.

Effective school-based assessment:

  • enables students to demonstrate what they know, understand and can do
  • is inclusive of, and accessible for, all students
  • is valid: there is clear alignment between the syllabus, the assessment activity and the criteria used to assess
  • identifies strengths, misunderstandings and skills not yet mastered
  • enables timely and relevant feedback about learning progress
  • provides opportunities for students to reflect on feedback
  • is regular, purposeful and integrated throughout teaching and learning
  • informs goal setting for learning and teaching.

Teachers should evaluate the effectiveness of their assessment approaches regularly to ensure they are fit for purpose. Reviewing student work in relation to assessment activities can provide useful information for decision-making.

Decisions teachers make about teaching, learning and assessment include:

  • what outcomes will be assessed in relation to the content that has been taught
  • why assessment will occur at a point in time and for what purpose
  • how information about student learning will be gathered and what approach will be used
  • how the information will be used, including to provide feedback, and to determine student progress and achievement
  • what next steps will inform future teaching and learning.

Standards-referenced assessment

Standards-referenced assessment refers to the process of interpreting information about student learning in relation to standards. It is used to compare student performance to a standard with objective criteria rather than to the performance of other students. Standards-referenced assessment can provide meaningful feedback about student achievement and support consistent assessment and reporting.

What are standards?

A standards-referenced approach is used to assess and report student achievement in NSW. This approach comprises 2 components:

  • syllabus outcomes and content describe what students are expected to learn
  • how well students demonstrate achievement is described in performance standards such as the Common Grade Scale.

Syllabus outcomes are used by teachers to:

  • plan and develop learning and assessment opportunities in relation to content
  • assess student progress and achievement in relation to intended learning
  • report student progress and achievement at key points in time.

Performance standards used to report student achievement in NSW include:

  • Common Grade Scale (Years 1 to 10)
  • Stage 5 Course Performance Descriptors (end of Year 10)
  • Common Grade Scale for preliminary courses (Year 11)
  • HSC Performance Band Descriptions (Year 12)
  • achievement level descriptions (Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1, and Numeracy).

It is not a requirement for student reports in Early Stage 1 to refer to a performance standard such as a grade scale. More information on standards-referenced reporting is available in Reporting and using grades.

Inclusive assessment

Approaches to assessment should be inclusive of all students. Assessment design should consider the ways students engage in the activity, how information is presented and accessed, and the different ways that students can demonstrate their understanding. Inclusive assessment means ensuring all students are able to demonstrate their learning.

Inclusive assessment considers the following:

  • How students engage:
    • developing accessible learning goals and criteria
    • integrating student choice, for example allowing students to choose topics or contexts in which they demonstrate learning
    • simulating real-life contexts that have explicit relevance to students.
  • How information is presented and accessed, including:
    • resources and/or stimulus material that is presented across a range of modes and that include accessibility options
    • both digital and non-digital resources.
  • How students respond:
    • using self-paced activities that support students to demonstrate learning without time constraints
    • providing opportunities for students to make choices about how they communicate their learning
    • providing opportunities to challenge and/or extend students within their level of understanding.

Adjustments for students with disability

It is a requirement under the Disability Standards for Education 2005 for schools to ensure that assessment tasks are accessible to students with disability. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access assessment activities and tasks and to demonstrate their learning. In some cases, this may mean providing an alternative assessment activity. Schools are responsible for any decisions made at school level to offer adjustments to assessment activities and tasks, including in-school tests. Decisions regarding adjustments should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Determining grades

A standards-referenced approach is used to report student achievement in NSW. Achievement standards are based on what students are expected to learn and how well they have achieved.

The NSW syllabuses state the intended learning for students by the end of each stage. A to E grade scales describe how well students have achieved. Teachers make professional on-balance judgements to decide which grade description best matches the standards their students have achieved at a particular point in time. These decisions are based on evidence of achievement and information teachers have collected during the teaching and learning.

The A to E grade allocated to a student and reported on NESA credentials reflects the level of achievement demonstrated by the student at the end of the course.

Moderating grades

Teachers follow a process of ‘moderation’ to ensure that grades allocated are consistent with published standards. This means that the grade a student receives in one school can be compared to the same grade anywhere in NSW.

Teachers moderate their judgements by comparing work samples for their students with samples aligned to grades A to E.

Choosing the right grade

Reporting with grades requires that teachers use on-balance judgement in relation to standards. This is a key professional skill.

An on-balance judgement does not just focus on a single piece of work or solely on test results.

Teachers should weigh up the evidence of achievement and other information collected for a student up to that point in time. This information is derived from learning activities, observations and other methods of assessment that are collected over time and in different situations. For further information read our Assessment principles page.

Making on-balance professional judgments involves considering all available evidence of student achievement, with an emphasis on identifying the descriptors that best reflect each student’s performance by the end of the course. Relying solely on marks and predetermined cut scores to allocate grades can lead to inaccuracies, especially for students who demonstrate significant progress over time and are performing at a higher level at the course’s conclusion than they were earlier in the course.

Students with disability

Students with disability may require adjustments to assessment activities to enable access to the activities and equitable opportunity to demonstrate what they know and can do. Students with disability who receive adjustments to assessment activities should have access to the full range of grades.

Using student work samples

Schools can use student work samples to strengthen their understanding of standards. NESA provides limited work samples aligned to A to E grades for a selection of learning areas to assist teachers in understanding state-wide standards. Available work samples can be found with the syllabuses.

Schools can use these published work samples to moderate the grades they allocate to students by comparing the standards of work published with those produced by their students in the same or similar learning areas.

Schools can also use samples of work from their own students for professional development with their staff and/or teachers from other schools. These work samples can provide the basis for professional discussions about standards and ensure there are consistent expectations about student achievement in relation to syllabus outcomes.

Reviewing and improving assessment activities

Referring to student work from previous years may assist teachers to clarify what is expected prior to the grading or marking of student work. Reviewing student work samples may also provide useful information about assessment activities that could lead to improvements in task design. For example, if an assessment activity is found to provide limited opportunities for students to demonstrate achievement at grade A, this could inform future assessment activities so that they are designed with increased scope for students to demonstrate higher levels of knowledge, understanding and skills in relation to the relevant grade scale or achievement level descriptions.

Determining Stage 5 grades

Assessing student achievement is the process of collecting information on student performance in relation to the objectives and outcomes of a course.

In setting activities or tasks, teachers should give careful consideration to the syllabus objectives and outcomes being assessed. By measuring student achievement in relation to these objectives and outcomes, teachers can build up a profile of the achievement of each student in relation to the course performance descriptors.

Grading student achievement is the process of assigning a letter (A, B, C, D, E) to summarise the level of a student's achievement in a course. For students undertaking courses without subject-specific course performance descriptors, that is, Board Endorsed or Content Endorsed Courses, a grade from A to E should be assigned using the Common Grade Scale.

Establishing an assessment program

In establishing an assessment program, teachers should ensure that the types of assessment activities or tasks used are appropriate to the objectives and outcomes being assessed. Generally, it will be necessary to use a number of different assessment activities or tasks in order to ensure that student achievement in relation to all the knowledge and skills objectives is assessed. Principals have the authority to decide on and to implement disability provisions for school-based assessments and tests.

The assessment program should also reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Where activities or tasks are scheduled throughout a course, greater weight would generally be given to those activities or tasks undertaken towards the end of the course. For example, in a 200-hour course extending over Years 9 and 10, the assessment information collected in Year 10 provides the more complete picture of student achievement. There are, however, a number of different ways of organising the teaching/learning program for a course. The scheduling of activities or tasks and the weights applied should reflect the course organisation. Students should be given the opportunity to demonstrate their maximum level of achievement relative to the course performance descriptors.

Applying the course performance descriptors

Course performance descriptors have been developed for each course. They describe the main features of a typical student's performance at each grade measured against the syllabus objectives and outcomes for the course.

Teachers will make the final judgement of the most appropriate grade on the basis of all available assessment information and with reference to the course performance descriptors. In applying these descriptors, teachers should interpret them in terms of standards that can be achieved by Stage 5 students within the bounds of the course. The same course performance descriptors apply to 100-hour and 200-hour courses. This relates to courses studied across Years 9 and 10, and to courses studied exclusively in either Year 9 or Year 10.

The grades allocated should reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Advice for Year 12: English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC

Schools must allocate to students who complete Year 12 English Studies or Mathematics Standard 1, or Numeracy CEC the grade that reflects their achievement at the end of the course. This grade is reported on the student’s HSC Record of Achievement.

To ensure grades have consistent meaning across the state, NESA monitors the grades allocated and reviews student work samples provided by schools.

Checklist for schools

This checklist relates to Year 12 grades that are reported on students' NESA credentials.

1. Read the Achievement Level Descriptions

Familiarise yourself with the Achievement Level Descriptions, on the syllabus page for the relevant course.

  • English Studies Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Mathematics Standard 1 Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Numeracy CEC Achievement Level Descriptions

2. Review work samples

Samples of student work aligned to grades are provided on the syllabus page. Use the samples and their annotations to get a clear understanding of the standard at each grade.

3. Upload grades and work samples

  • Decide on the appropriate grade for each student based on the achievement they have demonstrated at the end of the course.
  • Enter student grades in Schools Online.
  • Upload student work samples and the associated assessment activities in Schools Online.

Schools Online has guides on how to enter grades and upload student work samples. Learn more about submitting work samples.

4. Confirm grades

Check the grades entered in Schools Online are correct before they are confirmed by the principal.

5. Revise grades

Schools may be contacted by NESA and asked to revise grades. If your school is contacted, you will have a short period of time to make changes.

6. Keep grades confidential

NESA monitors grades before they are finalised and released to students. School assessment grades are available to students in Students Online once the final HSC exam has ended. Do not reveal grades to students before this time.
